roles-system-user-assistant.title: Roles in the chat format
roles-system-user-assistant.description: What "system", "user" and "assistant" actually are once the message list is flattened into tokens.

steps.heading: What your code sends
steps.caption: The message list — your application sends structured messages, each tagged with a role.

steps.heading: After templating and tokenisation
steps.caption: The chat template — the list is flattened into one token sequence with special role markers. This is what the model really sees.

steps.heading: In-policy response
steps.caption: Generation — the model continues from the assistant marker, and everything before it is context it conditions on.

steps.heading: Request 3 of a conversation
steps.caption: Multi-turn — prior assistant turns are re-sent as context on every request. The model has no memory between calls; your app supplies it.

steps.heading: An override attempt
steps.caption: Not a security boundary — a user message can contradict the system prompt, and sometimes wins. Roles steer behaviour; they do not enforce it.

zero-one-few-shot.title: Zero-, one- and few-shot prompting
zero-one-few-shot.description: The same task with 0, 1 and 3 in-context examples — and what each one costs and buys.

steps.heading: Assembled prompt: 38 tokens
steps.caption: Zero-shot — instruction only. It works when the task is common and the output format is easy to describe in words.

steps.heading: Three runs of the same zero-shot prompt
steps.caption: Zero-shot output — correct label, wrong shape. Nothing in the instruction pinned down whether to return prose or a bare token.

steps.heading: Assembled prompt: 61 tokens
steps.caption: One-shot — a single demonstration is inserted before the query. It shows the format far more precisely than a sentence describing it.

steps.heading: Assembled prompt: 107 tokens
steps.caption: Few-shot — three examples covering all three labels. Coverage matters more than count: show each class at least once.

steps.heading: Parseable-output rate versus number of examples
steps.caption: Diminishing returns — format compliance jumps with the first example or two, then flattens while cost keeps climbing.

self-consistency.title: Self-consistency
self-consistency.description: Sample several independent reasoning paths, throw away the reasoning, and take a majority vote on the answers.

steps.heading: The question
steps.caption: A problem where one reasoning slip changes the answer — several arithmetic steps, each a chance to go wrong.

steps.heading: 5 independent chain-of-thought samples
steps.caption: Sample N paths independently at temperature 0.7. Because sampling is stochastic, each run reasons slightly differently.

steps.heading: Final answers extracted from the 5 samples
steps.caption: Extract only the final answers — the reasoning text is discarded. The vote is over conclusions, not explanations.

steps.heading: Vote share
steps.caption: Majority vote — ₹195 wins 3–1–1. The mistakes were uncorrelated, so they split their votes and the correct answer stayed modal.

steps.heading: Accuracy and cost versus number of samples
steps.caption: Cost and limits — accuracy rises with N and then flattens, while you pay N times per question. And correlated errors defeat it entirely.

tree-of-thoughts.title: Tree of Thoughts
tree-of-thoughts.description: Search instead of a single line of reasoning: propose several next steps, score them, keep the promising ones, go deeper.

steps.heading: Game of 24: reach 24 using 4, 9, 10, 13 exactly once each
steps.caption: The root — a planning problem where the first move constrains everything after it, so committing early is risky.

steps.heading: Depth 1: four candidate first operations
steps.caption: Propose — generate several candidate first steps rather than one. Breadth at depth 1.

steps.heading: Self-evaluated promise of each branch
steps.caption: Evaluate — the model scores each partial state for how likely it is to reach a solution. This is the step CoT does not have.

steps.heading: Depth 2, expanded only under the survivors
steps.caption: Prune and expand — keep the top 2, drop the rest, and generate the next layer only under the survivors.

steps.heading: Cost of the three reasoning strategies on this problem
steps.caption: Solution and cost — a leaf reaches 24. It took roughly 14 model calls where chain-of-thought would have used one.

react-prompting.title: ReAct as a prompt format
react-prompting.description: Before it is a runtime, ReAct is a text convention: the model writes Thought / Action / Observation lines and your parser reads them.

steps.heading: System prompt excerpt
steps.caption: The format is taught in the prompt — you describe the Thought/Action/Observation convention and list the available tools.

steps.heading: Model output, verbatim
steps.caption: The model writes Thought and Action, then stops. "Observation:" is configured as a stop sequence, so generation halts there.

steps.heading: Who does what
steps.caption: Your runtime parses the Action line, executes the real tool, and appends the result as an Observation. Then generation resumes.

steps.heading: Real drift seen in production
steps.caption: Parsing is the fragile part — the model drifts from the format, and a strict parser then fails on perfectly reasonable output.

steps.heading: Trade-offs
steps.caption: What it buys — grounded answers plus a readable trace. What it costs — every thought is billed as tokens and may leak reasoning to the user.

prompt-chaining.title: Prompt chaining
prompt-chaining.description: One hard task split into staged calls, with a real artifact handed from each stage to the next.

steps.heading: Single mega-prompt
steps.caption: The monolith — one prompt asked to extract, draft, check compliance and format all at once. It usually does three of the four.

steps.heading: Chain stage 1
steps.caption: Stage 1, extract — a narrow call with a structured output. The artifact is data your code can inspect, not prose.

steps.heading: Chain stage 2 — fan out
steps.caption: Stage 2, draft — 23 requirements means 23 independent calls that can run in parallel, cutting wall-clock latency.

steps.heading: Compliance check results
steps.caption: Stage 3, validate — a separate call checks each draft. Failures are caught here and retried, not discovered by a customer.

steps.heading: When to split a prompt
steps.caption: The trade-off — more calls, more latency to manage, more code. In exchange you get testable, cacheable, individually swappable stages.

structured-outputs.title: Structured outputs and constrained decoding
structured-outputs.description: The difference between asking politely for JSON and making invalid JSON impossible to sample.

steps.heading: 100 runs of a prompt that asks for JSON
steps.caption: Asking nicely — an instruction to "return JSON only" works most of the time, and most of the time is not good enough for a parser.

steps.heading: Invoice extraction schema
steps.caption: The schema — declare the exact fields and types you need. Keep it minimal; every optional field is another chance to drift.

steps.heading: p(next token) after "{", no constraint
steps.caption: Unconstrained sampling — after the opening brace, tokens like "Sure" and a newline still carry real probability. Any of them breaks the parse.

steps.heading: Same step, with the JSON grammar applied
steps.caption: Constrained decoding — invalid tokens get a logit of −∞ before the softmax, so their probability is exactly zero and the rest renormalise.

steps.heading: The full pattern
steps.caption: Still validate — the grammar guarantees shape, not sense. A syntactically perfect object can hold a hallucinated total.

role-prompting-constraints.title: Personas versus constraints
role-prompting-constraints.description: One of these two changes measurable behaviour. It is not the one people spend their time on.

steps.heading: Persona only
steps.caption: The persona — sets tone and vocabulary. Useful, but it makes no promise you can test in an evaluation suite.

steps.heading: Same prompt, constraints added
steps.caption: The constraints — rules with an observable pass/fail. Each one can become an assertion in your test suite.

steps.heading: Rule-compliance rate over 200 runs
steps.caption: Measured effect — the persona barely moves compliance. The constraints move it a lot, because they say what "correct" means.

steps.heading: A collision
steps.caption: Conflicts need a stated priority — when the persona and a safety rule disagree, the prompt must say which one wins.

steps.heading: Defence in depth for one rule
steps.caption: And enforce outside the prompt — a constraint in the system message is a strong hint; a validator in code is a guarantee.

context-engineering.title: Context engineering
context-engineering.description: Selecting, ordering and compressing what enters the window — including where in the window each piece lands.

steps.heading: Candidate context for one coding question
steps.caption: Inventory — list everything that could go into the window, with its token cost. Most of it will not make the cut.

steps.heading: Measured effect of including each source (ablation)
steps.caption: Rank by expected effect on the answer — not by how related the material feels. Test output beats chat history here.

steps.heading: Packed window
steps.caption: Compress rather than drop — the chat history becomes a short summary, keeping the useful part at a fraction of the cost.

steps.heading: Answer accuracy versus where the needed fact sits in a long context
steps.caption: Position matters — the same evidence is used far more reliably at the start or end of a long context than buried in the middle.

steps.heading: Final layout of the window
steps.caption: Order deliberately — instructions first, evidence next with the best passage last, then the question immediately before generation.

prompt-failure-modes.title: How prompts fail
prompt-failure-modes.description: Four failure modes with distinct symptoms, and the measurement that tells them apart.

steps.heading: Output length across 20 runs of "Write a promo email. Make it pop."
steps.caption: Ambiguity — "make it pop" has no measurable target, so the model picks a different interpretation each run.

steps.heading: Contradictory instructions
steps.caption: Instruction conflict — two rules that cannot both hold. The model satisfies one at random, so behaviour looks flaky rather than wrong.

steps.heading: JSON compliance versus input length
steps.caption: Format drift under load — a prompt that is reliable on short inputs starts dropping the format on long ones.

steps.heading: Same prompt, two model versions
steps.caption: Model upgrade regression — a prompt tuned against one model breaks on its successor, because the assumptions it encoded were about that model.

steps.heading: Output length variance, before and after
steps.caption: The fix is specificity plus testing — replace adjectives with measurable constraints, then keep a regression set that runs on every change.

chain-of-thought.title: Chain of thought
chain-of-thought.description: Ask the model to write intermediate reasoning before the answer — a single path, not a search tree.

steps.heading: No CoT
steps.caption: Direct answer — the model jumps to a number. For multi-step arithmetic that often fails silently.

steps.heading: Added instruction
steps.caption: CoT instruction — “show your steps” forces intermediate tokens that structure the computation.

steps.heading: One chain
steps.caption: Reasoning path — each line is sampled text that becomes context for the next line.

steps.heading: Limit
steps.caption: Still one path — if step 2 multiplies wrong, the final answer is wrong with a convincing story.
